1:
Where the false prophets were is the first question. Gill allows either those in the land, of whom the prophet had notice, or rather those among the captives where he then was. Calvin decides for the exiles and describes their trade: among the captives were men who assumed the name of God and boasted the prophetic spirit while intruding into the office, and their end was to promise a speedy return and so win the favour of the multitude; the captives were already almost broken-hearted with weariness, and seventy years was a long period, so that when they heard of returning after three years they easily suffered themselves to be deceived by such blandishments. Henry places them in both quarters, and notes the symmetry, that as the true prophets, though separated in place or time, preached the same truths and so showed themselves guided by one good Spirit, the false ones prophesied the same lies, being actuated by one and the same spirit of error. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same double answer another way: they are to be sought not merely among the exiles but principally among those left behind in the land, since a lively intercourse was kept up between the two.

Calvin will not let the charge exempt the people. Though God is so vehemently enraged against the impostors, it does not follow that he absolves the hearers or even extenuates their fault. They could not object that they were deceived, since they willingly and knowingly threw themselves into the snare: they were not destitute of true prophets, and God had distinguished his servants from the false by well-known marks, so that no one could mistake except willfully. In the midst of light they blinded themselves, and God suffered them to be deceived, which was the just reward of a pride that could not be subject to him or his servants; and when they wanted enticements, God gave the reins to Satan, so that there was a lying spirit in the mouth of all the prophets. Calvin adds the complaint of another prophet, that they desired prophets who should promise large grape-gatherings and a plentiful harvest, and roared when God chastised them severely.

Henry states the purpose of a message to men past persuading. There were little hopes of bringing them to repentance, so hardened were they in their sin, yet the prophet must speak, in hopes that the people might be cautioned not to hearken to them, and so that a testimony would be left upon record against them and they left inexcusable. He notes the irony in the title: they called themselves the prophets of Israel as if none but they deserved the name, being indeed the deceivers of Israel; and he observes that the nation was never imposed upon by pretenders to prophecy until after it had rejected and abused the true prophets. They took upon them to speak what concerned others as from God, Henry says; let them now hear what concerns themselves as from him.

Prophesying out of their own hearts is glossed by three. Gill notes that they were so called and so accounted, though not true but false prophets, and that the Targum names them so. Wesley says they spoke out of their own deceiving hearts and not from God. Clarke presses the point: they are neither inspired nor sent, having their mission from their own assumption and proceeding in it from their own presumption, so that they either go of themselves or are sent by man. Clarke also gives the plan of the chapter: judgments against those who flattered the people with false hopes of peace, the work of the deceivers compared to a frail and insolent piece of building which can never stand against the battering elements of heaven, and the woes denounced at the end against the women who practised vain rites for their own gain.
3:
Being called foolish is felt as the sting. Gill says it must have been a great mortification to men who reckoned themselves wise and were accounted so by others, since what is wisdom with men is foolishness with God. Ellicott says they were certainly foolish who undertook to forge the name of the Omniscient to utterances of their own devising, and notes that in the older usage folly was never merely an intellectual failing but was always associated with moral obliquity; he prefers the marginal rendering of the last clause, that they were seers of what they had not seen. Calvin weighs the word, which can mean a vile person or a castaway as well as a fool, and takes the commoner sense. He explains the charge by their conduct, since they fiercely insulted the true servants of God like upstarts puffed up with self-conceit and wished to be thought angels come down from heaven, the devil who reigns in them being the father of pride; he grants that human fictions have a form of wisdom, so that these pretenders were held in great esteem, and yet the Spirit pronounces them fools. Wesley states the rule behind it: whom God sends he either finds fit or makes fit, and where he gives warrant he gives wisdom.

The foxes are read for cunning, for hunger, or for habitation. Gill takes them for craft and for lying in wait to deceive, and reports Kimchi taking the deserts as breaches and ruinous places in the walls of a vineyard, by which foxes enter to spoil it. Clarke keeps to the cunning and gives the figure a sharper turn: as the fox carries his prey to the desert to hide both himself and it, so the false prophets got out of the way when the event did not answer their prediction, that they might not be overwhelmed with the reproaches of the people. Ellicott holds the comparison close enough if taken only of mischievous men living unconcerned among the ruins of their country, as foxes find their home in desolated cities, though many extend the simile to the undermining of the ground. Calvin builds the image out: the dispersed people were like a vineyard removed into desert regions where foxes held sway, since while they dwelt at home they were fortified as by ramparts and a high priest presided over spiritual trials at the capital, whereas now the miserable exiles lay open to injury as if deserts surrounded them. He turns it into a reproof of the people, who ought to have been attentive and cautious, since God promises the spirit of discretion to those who need it.

The gaps are where the failure is named. Gill takes the allusion from breaches made in a besieged wall, where those within gather in great numbers to prevent the entrance of the enemy, and applies it either to the civil magistrates or to the prophets, who seeing the sins of the people open a breach for judgment should have pressed them to repentance and made intercession for them. Wesley draws the same picture and says the standing meant is not with arms but with fasting, prayer and repentance. Clarke says they did the opposite, preventing repentance by their flattering promises, and contributed nothing by prayers, example or advice. Ellicott corrects one rendering, which should be wall rather than hedge, and says the whole language is figurative, the breaches in the material walls representing the moral decay of the people; these prophets, like the hireling shepherds of a later parable, were only selfish and had no care for the flock. Calvin restricts the verse to their teaching, against those who refer it to prayer, and states the mark of a true servant: to consult the public safety, and when the signs of wrath appear, to meet them and prevent the urgent calamity.
6:
Calvin makes the vanity follow from the source. Nothing false or vain can proceed from God, so that men who spoke from their own heart are condemned of vanity and lying because they dared falsely to use the name of God when they uttered nothing but their own dreams. Gill says the same, that the visions were the fruit of their own fancies and the predictions lies that never came to pass; Wesley calls them things that have no foundation.

Calvin then draws the distinction that gives the chapter its edge. True prophets also recall sinners to the mercy of God and magnify it, so that those wrestling with despair may not doubt his long-suffering, since his pity is said to endure for a life while his anger passes away in a moment. But they join two members which must not be separated: when they exhort sinners to hope and predict a freeness to pardon, they discourse also about penitence, and do not indulge sinners but rouse them, wounding them sharply with a sense of anger, since mercy is set before us to the end that by it we may seek life, so that we must first be dead in ourselves. The false prophets sever the two and divide God, as it were, in half, puffing up the people with the vain hope that he would not be so severe as to exact continual punishment of an elect nation.

Using the name is the aggravation. Calvin says they created darkness out of light, since that sacred name is a fount of splendour surpassing the light of the sun, and yet by the feint of speaking in it they darkened the minds of men. To boast that God has spoken, he says, is as if one wished by impious profanation to draw him purposely into a dispute, for how can he bear us to turn his truth into a lie? Such impostors have existed in every age, and are no surprise among the heathen; but among a people who had access to all heavenly doctrine, and to whom prophets were daily called forth, it was an incredible prodigy and an intolerable disgrace. Gill puts the contrast between the two utterances shortly: this is what the Lord says, and may be depended on to come to pass, whereas the other he did not say, though they said he did.

The sentence divides into three exclusions. Calvin observes that the threat of God becoming an adversary is not by itself enough to terrify men so stupid, which is why the hand is brought forward, the hand being sometimes taken for a blow; and he explains that such carelessness would not have besotted the impious unless they thought themselves free of all dealings with God. On the first exclusion he rejects a subtler reading of the word for assembly, which some take of the experience of God offered to the elect for their salvation, calling it forced, since the second clause repeats the same thing in different words; the word signifies a secret and so is taken for counsel, and the catalogue is named because judges and others elected to office were written in a list. Wesley gives the three plainly: no seat among the rulers nor voice among the counsellors, no registration among those that return, and no entrance into the land; and he reports the paraphrast adding that they shall not be written in the book of eternal life. Clarke says they shall not be reputed members of the Church nor reckoned in the genealogy of the true Israelites that return, but shall be expatriated and perish in the siege by sword, famine and pestilence. Ellicott notes that the original word bears the marginal senses too but that the text is correct here, and that the clauses together emphasise the utter exclusion of these men from the people of God.
10:
The lie is peace where there is none. Henry sets out what it amounted to: they pretended visions of peace, told the people that God was at peace with them and had mercy in reserve, and told idolaters and other sinners that there was neither harm nor danger in the way they were in. So they drew the people out of the way of repentance which the other prophets were labouring to bring them into; and Henry adds the rule, repeated by Wesley, that those are the most dangerous seducers who suggest to sinners what tends to lessen their dread of sin and their fear of God. Gill limits the deception, since those who are truly the people of God may be deceived in civil things but not totally and finally in religious matters, so that the seduced are the people by profession.

The wall and the daubing are worked out at length. Clarke makes a true prophet a wall of defence to the people, and says these men pretended to be such a wall, but their wall is bad and their mortar worse: one gives a lying vision and another pledges that it is true, which is like daubing a bad wall with bad mortar, preventing its blemishes from being discovered while doing nothing to strengthen the building. Ellicott distinguishes the two words used, the first a partition wall and comparatively slight, the second the ordinary word for a city wall; and he traces the word for the plaster through its other occurrences, where it means unsavoury, or foolish things, or folly, noting that though it must mean plaster here, its use elsewhere shows what sort is meant. He cites Calvin as understanding it of mortar mixed with sand and water only, the lime left out, and observes that it is still a common practice in the East to cover walls with stucco.

Calvin makes the figure a development of the earlier one. Teachers who discharge their duty honestly are like builders who repair a breach as soon as they see it, and like gardeners who will not let a vineyard lie open to wild beasts; he had said these men did not go up to the breach, and now grants them more, that they really built. The two are easy to reconcile, since they did not build for the safety of the people and yet feigned themselves anxious, as if they wished to restore the ruins. But he grants only their intention, and adds that they were bad builders. Henry compares the whole to the building of a slight rotten wall; Wesley calls the mortar sorry stuff that will not bind nor hold the bricks together, and names what it stands for, doctrines not grounded on the word of God.

The storm that levels it is read as the event itself. Clarke notes that in eastern countries, where walls are built with unbaked bricks, tempestuous rains often cause such desolations, and that ancient city walls were made of this material, which is why no vestige of them remains. Ellicott observes that hail is unusual in that country though its destructive effects were well known. Calvin says the shower means a violent concussion that shall disperse all their artifices and detect their frauds when the city is delivered up, and that the same thing had to be expressed in many ways because the people had grown torpid through their fallacies. On the question that follows the fall, Calvin says these men shall be subject to the greatest ridicule when convicted by the event, so that a common proverb would arise. Ellicott says the same: the basis of their false prophesying being destroyed by the coming judgments, those who made the people trust in it shall be overwhelmed in its ruin. Gill puts it in three words, that the falling of the wall is the taking of the city.
13:
These four verses repeat what has been said, and Calvin defends the repetition. He grants that the prophet would seem too verbose, since he might have said in a few words what he explains at such length; but if the perverse and refractory disposition of the people be borne in mind, there was need of such continual repetition. The false prophets had acquired so much favour that their boasting was esteemed as an oracle, and the people were persuaded that even what these impostors dreamt was uttered by God; having so bound the minds of men to themselves, they could not be answered by simple language. Gill says the same more briefly, that the words are repeated both for confirmation and for explanation of what went before.

The storm is now sent rather than foretold. Calvin notes that hail and showers and violent storms had been spoken of already, and that the difference here is only that God shows more clearly that he will send them forth, the winds and storms and showers standing at hand to obey him and overthrow the empty building these men had raised. Gill takes the accomplishing of wrath upon the wall as the pouring out of all indignation upon the city and its inhabitants, and reports the Targum reading the wall as the city outright; Wesley glosses the accomplishing as the fulfilling of what the true prophets foretold.

What the uncovered foundation means is the chief point with Calvin. God would so lay bare the fallacies of those who had deceived the people with vain hopes that no disguise should remain for them, and their disgrace be plain to every one. He describes the shamelessness he is answering: convicted on one point, these men did not desist on that account, but took credit whenever anything turned out more fortunately than they could expect, as if they had not prophesied in vain while a single thing came true. Therefore, he says, they would have nothing left, since God would not only overthrow whatever they seemed to build but leave them nothing to fall back on. Wesley draws the moral: those who deceived others will in the end be found to have deceived themselves, and no doom will be more fearful than that of unfaithful ministers.

Calvin closes the section by dating the deceit to the life of the city. While it stood, the appearance of a wall existed, for there was the prop of false doctrine and the people fed willingly on such deceits; their daubing stood until it vanished with the ruin of the city, and then their vanity was proved. He adds that God suffered them to triumph among the people only for a short time, though even to the destruction of the city and temple they withstood his servants with a bold forehead. On the last verse he distinguishes the men in view from those a contemporary prophet contended with at home, taking them for the men who in exile still hardened the wretched, stirring up to pride a people already grievously wounded by the hand of God. And he answers the apparent contradiction between seeing nothing and seeing visions of peace: they were altogether without the Spirit and had no revelation, but since they boasted themselves endowed with it and many had faith in their words, the prophet concedes them the name of a vision by accommodation. Gill notes only that the verse explains who was meant by those that daubed.
17:
That there were true prophetesses is what makes the false ones possible, and every voice says so. Gill names three from the older history who had the true spirit of prophecy and one from the time of the return who pretended to it. Clarke reasons from the principle that as a false religion necessarily implies a true one of which it is the ape, so false prophetesses necessarily imply true ones whom they endeavoured to imitate, and he lists five true ones. Calvin says the gift is sometimes, though rarely, allowed to women, and offers a reason: when the sister of Moses enjoyed it, that never ceased to be a reproach to her brother, and when the two later women discharged the office, God wished to raise them on high to shame the men and obliquely show them their slothfulness. Henry sets the promise beside the abuse: as God has promised that when he pours out his Spirit both sons and daughters shall prophesy, so the devil, acting as a spirit of lies, is in the mouth of false prophetesses as well as false prophets. Calvin puts the same point as the method of Satan, who emulates God and transforms himself into an angel of light, since if he showed himself openly all would instantly flee from him.

Henry insists the sex is neither an excuse nor a shelter. These are not such despicable enemies of the truth as deserve to be passed over, and neither will the weakness of the sex excuse their sin nor the respect owing to it exempt them from the threatenings of the word. He notes what setting the face means: the prophet must try whether they can look him in the face and stand to what they say; and he draws the rule that when sinners grow very impudent it is time for reprovers to be very bold.

The pillows and the kerchiefs are described in different ways. Gill reads the pillows as a signal that the hearers might be at ease and secure and fear no invasion. Wesley takes them as a figure for the security promised to every one that came, and the kerchiefs as triumphal caps put on the head of each enquirer to promise victory, the mention of stature meaning every age, whether younger or elder. Clarke thinks of the cushions provided in the apartments of the East, on which women sit and lean and prop up their arms, and takes the whole for the state of softness to which these predictions allured the city, a careless voluptuous life being what is reprehended; on the second word he corrects the English, since a kerchief is properly what covers the head, and reports that Calmet takes the term for a kind of hunting net, which suits the use it is put to here.

Calvin explains the apparatus as a technique. There is no doubt that by these tricks they deluded the minds and eyes of the simple; some ceremonies are useful, since God commands nothing superfluous, but Satan by his cunning turns everything useful to the destruction of men. He adds that false prophets were always immoderately fond of outward signs, since having nothing substantial to offer they need ostentation to dazzle all eyes, which is why those who intend to deceive heap together a number of ceremonies. He supposes the pillows were laid under the arms of those who consulted them, in imitation of the ancient manner of reclining at table, to represent a kind of sleep, like men who consult oracles and think themselves in ecstasies snatched away beyond all thoughts of this world; and he compares the veiled head of the Roman augur, who stood at the threshold with his head covered and began his incantations. Ellicott adds only that the word for souls, which bears a variety of senses, is here nearly equivalent to persons.
19:
The handfuls of barley are the measure of the offence. Ellicott explains the ancient custom of bringing presents to a prophet on consulting him, and notes that since barley was a cheap grain and handfuls a very small quantity, the words show the exceedingly small gains for which these women were willing to pervert the truth. Gill says the same, that they drew the people from the fear and worship of God for gain, and for small gain too; Wesley calls it a mean reward. On the polluting, Gill says the name was defiled by being used to cover wicked designs, reports the Targum reading it as polluting the will of God among his people, and adds that to profane the name among the Gentiles was a great sin but among his own people greater.

Calvin makes the sacrilege the heavier of two crimes. The first was cruelly to destroy the souls that were sacred to God and destined to be saved; the second, more atrocious, was to abuse the name of God to deceive, since nothing is less tolerable than turning the truth of God into a lie, which is like reducing him to nothing. God is truth, and if that is abolished what remains behind but a dead spectre? He grounds the argument in the gift itself: prophecy was a rare and remarkable pledge of divine love, and God was never willing to be disjoined from his word, being invisible and appearing only as in a mirror, so that his glory and holiness and justice and power ought to shine in that gift; when it is contaminated, the disgrace becomes a reproach against him. Ellicott states the same in a sentence, that God was polluted by the attaching of his name and authority to what was not true and would not come to pass, making him a liar like themselves.

The double harm is noticed by two. Ellicott says their lies tended both ways, to entice the upright to their ruin and to give false security to the wicked, and that it is always impossible for a perversion of the truth, especially in regard to the divine judgments, to be harmless; on the last clause he prefers to hearken to a lie, the words implying a willingness to listen to the pleasing falsehood, and he quotes the earlier prophet on a people who love to have it so. Wesley states it as a pair: they denounce evil to the best, whom God will keep alive, and declare safety to the worst, whom he will destroy.

The tearing away of the apparatus is the sentence. Gill says the pillows were not only abhorred but marked for destruction, their fallacies detected and their folly exposed to contempt, and has the kerchiefs torn from the heads of the women, their tricks discovered. Calvin says the same for both, that God would render them not only contemptible but ridiculous before the whole people, and that the masks had to be stripped away because the people were so fascinated by these silly things. On the hunting word he considers a rendering of perishing, but prefers to fly with the rest, thinking the reference is to lofty speculations, since false prophets boast of raising the minds of men aloft and curious hearers desire only that, so that the doctrines of the Law and the Gospel become insipid to them and subtleties alone delight them. Clarke reports a scholar taking the word for flower gardens, into which these women decoyed men where impure rites were performed, and elsewhere glosses the kerchiefs as nets or amulets. Keil and Delitzsch note that the threat answers point for point to the reproof. Calvin closes on the promise of deliverance, restricting the people delivered to the elect, since many boasted themselves of the stock who were very unlike their father and by degenerating deprived themselves of the honour.
22:
Making the heart of the righteous sad raises a difficulty, and Calvin faces it. By the righteous he means those whom the false prophets inspired with causeless terror; but if none were deceived except those who threw themselves willingly into the snares, how can the righteous be grieved? He answers that these men thundered so, and scattered their threats so widely, that the simple were involved, since the threats were made to reach all men and so wounded weak consciences. When lies of that kind fly about, many simple people are frightened, being destitute of judgment and unable to distinguish whether God threatens or a man vaunts himself rashly; and so the righteous are made sorrowful, scruples being suggested to them and one thing after another denounced under the penalty of mortal sin, until they are deprived of confidence in the favour of God and struck with various terrors. Calvin notes that this explains the earlier and harder saying, that they slew the souls which ought not to die.

Gill and Clarke describe the same double effect. Gill names three ways the sadness was caused: by polluting the name of the Lord, by hunting and decoying souls into destructive nets, and by threatening those who would not give heed to their superstitious rites and lying divinations. Clarke states the whole ministry and its effect in two sentences: they would speak and had no truth to tell, and therefore spoke falsities; they saddened the souls of the righteous and strengthened the hands of the wicked, promising them life and preventing them from repenting and turning from their sins.

What the ending of their visions means is answered two ways. Gill offers both: either they should no longer be suffered to impose upon the people, being so sufficiently exposed that none would give heed to their vain visions any more, and no gain coming to them they would not care to pretend to them; or else they should perish in the siege and destruction of the city, so that they and their false prophecies would cease together. Wesley takes the first, that they shall see all their predictions vanish, and be so confounded that they shall pretend no more to visions.

Calvin insists the promise is not of a change in them. It ought not to be understood as if God promised these women a sound mind, so that they should cease to hurt the people by their lies; he is confirming what he said before, that they should be subject to the taunts of all, until even boys acknowledged that what they had boasted to be oracles was mere imposture. Though they persisted in their madness, they saw vanity no more, since it became openly apparent that the wretched people who trusted them had been deceived; so the words are to be adapted not to any change of feeling but to a failure of effect, as one might tell a foolish fellow who boasted himself a lawyer or a physician that he shall profit no more by either title, without his being able to put away the opinion he had formed of his own skill. Ellicott makes the same point from the shape of the sentence: the judgment is expressed in the same form as the sin, so that women who had sinned by lying visions should see them no more, because the event would soon expose their utter falsity to the eyes of all; the result would be the deliverance of the people they had sought to ensnare, and their own conviction, not in penitence but under judgment. Clarke closes on the alternative to true prophecy: where God is not, because of the iniquity of the people, the devil is, to strengthen and support that iniquity.
